title: Egress Acceleration + DNS Stub Strategy for Customer POC
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures a lightweight, operational-first design for accelerating egress and handling private DNS for the upcoming customer POC (large regulated customer with multi-AZ VPCs and strict outbound auditing). Goal: keep latency to external model caches <30ms median, avoid hairpinning, provide deterministic audit logs for egress, and allow quick fallbacks to hosted endpoints if private paths are congested.

Context and constraints (customer):
- VPC per environment (dev/stage/prod) across 3 regions (us-west-2, us-east-1, eu-west-1).
- Customer requires egress via their centralized NAT cluster for outbound inspection, but we need sub-50ms added latency for token-level streaming workloads.
- DNS must resolve internal endpoints for private model cache and fall back to Redwood-hosted endpoints under congestion.
- No change to customer outbound firewall rules for initial POC.

High-level approach (phased):
1) Onramp & proxy layer (phase 0/1):
   - Deploy lightweight regional edge proxies (k8s DaemonSet or small autoscaling group) inside customer VPC(s) close to worker subnets. Proxies are stateless, support HTTP/2 and gRPC, have local KV prefix-cache and TLS termination to Redwood endpoints.
   - Route application worker egress to local proxy via route table / iptables redirect. This keeps cross-AZ hairpin minimal.
   - Proxies should do TCP connection pooling to upstream Redwood endpoints to reduce TLS handshake per request.

2) Egress acceleration + NAT bypass (phase 1):
   - Where policy allows, configure proxies to use interface endpoints (AWS Global Accelerator or PrivateLink depending on account) to reach Redwood backplane directly, bypassing customer NAT for high-throughput flows.
   - For flows that must go through customer inspection (per compliance), proxy will mirror headers for auditing then forward via NAT. Use explicit per-prefix policy to mark traffic.

3) DNS stub & split-horizon strategy (phase 1/2):
   - Create DNS stub domain (e.g., .redwood-poc.internal) served by regional resolver instances. The stub domain maps private names to internal IPs (edge proxies, internal caches).
   - Use split-horizon for model hosts: inside customer VPC, model.redwood.ai -> internal accelerated VIP; external resolves to hosted API. TTLs should be short (15s) for quick failover.
   - If the resolver becomes unreachable, workers must detect NXDOMAIN/timeouts and failover to external hosts via configured fallback list.

4) Flow control and throughput shaping (phase 2):
   - Proxies implement token-aware batching windows for generation requests to reduce per-token overhead while meeting latency SLOs.
   - Rate limiter to ensure we do not saturate customer NAT or on-prem inspection appliances. Dynamic backpressure signalled to workers via 503+Retry-After and to Redwood controller via telemetry.

Design details and rationale:
- Why proxies? They allow connection reuse, prefix caching, local batching, and a point to implement split-horizon DNS and auditing without needing infra changes in worker apps.
- Why interface endpoints/privatelink? Bypassing NAT reduces jitter and egress cost; PrivateLink gives stable IPs and easier policy mapping for customer security teams.
- Short DNS TTL: enables quick rollbacks to hosted API or alternate region if a regional cache gets overloaded.
- Auditing: proxies emit structured JSON audit records (request id, originating instance, matched policy, bytes out, upstream endpoint) to S3 or to customer's SIEM over HTTPS.

Operational checklist for POC setup:
- Pre-PoC: confirm allowed IP ranges and whether PrivateLink can be established. Obtain certs and KMS access expectations.
- Infra: terraform to provision proxy ASGs / k8s manifests, interface endpoints, route table entries, and resolver instances.
- DNS: create hosted zone for stub domain, push resolver config to DHCP options (or use CoreDNS in VPC).
- Security: mutually authenticated mTLS between proxies and Redwood backplane; RBAC keys rotated for POC weekly.
- Monitoring: enable p99/p50 latency histograms, connection churn, TLS handshake rates, and audit log delivery metrics.

Example terraform-ish snippet (conceptual):
  # Conceptual proxy ASG + PrivateLink attachment
  resource "aws_lb_target_group" "proxy" {
    name = "redwood-proxy-tg"
    port = 443
    protocol = "HTTPS"
  }

  resource "aws_vpc_endpoint_service" "redwood_pl" {
    acceptance_required = true
    network_load_balancer_arns = [aws_lb.proxy.arn]
  }

Failure modes and mitigations:
- Resolver or proxy crash: workers fallback to system resolver and external hosted endpoints; short TTLs reduce caching impact.
- Customer NAT saturates: proxy signals backpressure; Redwood controller reduces batch sizes and routes to hosted fallback region.
- DNS split-horizon mismatch: add health-check-based override that forces external resolution when internal VIPs fail health checks.

Performance testing plan (minimal):
- Synthetic perf job generating streaming responses that emulate 8 token/sec per connection. Measure median/95/99 token latency with and without proxy.
- Run soak for 4 hours with gradual ramp to expected production concurrency. Monitor TLS churn, CPU/Sockets on proxy, NAT throughput.
- Failure injection: kill resolver, simulate high TTL cache and observe failover time.

Open questions / decisions required:
- Customer policy: is PrivateLink allowed in their org (some orgs deny new endpoints)? (ACTION: Ben to confirm with security contact by 2024-09-22)
- Audit delivery: S3 vs direct SIEM forward? Bandwidth/legal implications.
- Where should we run resolver? Small EC2 in each AZ or a k8s CoreDNS deployment? Tradeoffs: EC2 simpler, k8s easier to deploy with rest of proxy.

Next steps (short timeline):
- Week 0: alignment call with customer security/infra to confirm PrivateLink and NAT constraints (owner: Asha).
- Week 1: deploy dev proxies in us-west-2, low-scale tests, verify TLS & audit pipeline (owner: Priya).
- Week 2: run perf job, capture baseline, and iterate batching params (owner: Michael).
- Week 3: present results and recommendation: full PrivateLink + DNS stub or hosted fallback.

Notes to self / rough todos:
- Keep configuration options in terraform toggles: enable_privatelink = true, enable_audit_forward = "siem|s3".
- Add fallback list to workers via environment variable REDWOOD_EGRESS_FALLBACKS="https://api.redwood.ai,https://us-east-1.api.redwood.ai"
- Document rollback: remove route table entries pointing to proxy and restore original DHCP option set.

Unresolved technical risks:
- Packet MTU differences when traversing on-prem inspection appliances causing TLS fragmentation for streaming. Need to validate path MTU.
- DNS amplification of failures if TTL too short and upstream RRs rate-limit queries. Consider local caching with short eviction windows instead of zero TTL.

Appendix: quick checklist for customer kickoff (one-pager):
- Confirm PrivateLink acceptance
- Share firewall/NACLs + allowed ports (443/853 for DNS-over-TLS if needed)
- Provide list of subnets for proxy placement
- Agree audit delivery destination and retention
- Confirm MTU & packet inspection behaviors via test from customer infra team

End of doc.

(Informal notes and TODOs expect follow-ups; this is intentionally pragmatic and operator-facing — will be turned into a formal runbook if POC proceeds past week 3.)
